sections.title: Perimeter of a Circle — The C/D Ratio
Length of an Arc of a Circle
Problems, Puzzles, and Paradoxes on Perimeter

slides.title: Walk the Border
slides.kicker: An insect shows you what perimeter means
bullets: Perimeter is the total length around the border of any shape.
Imagine a tiny insect walking around the border, never turning back, till it returns to its starting point.
The total distance the insect travels is the perimeter of the shape.
Perimeter is a length, so it is measured in units like cm or m.
slides.note: Chalte chalte, the insect measures the whole boundary!

slides.title: Three Perimeter Formulas
slides.kicker: Square, triangle, rectangle in one breath
bullets: A square with side a units has perimeter 4a units.
An equilateral triangle with side a units has perimeter 3a units.
A rectangle with length a units and width b units has perimeter 2(a + b) units.
The square formula is a special case of the rectangle formula: put a = b and 2(a + b) becomes 4a.

right.title: Rectangle
items: square is the case a = b

slides.title: Same Shape, Same Ratio
slides.kicker: Double the side, double the perimeter
bullets: Double a square's side and its perimeter doubles too: side 2 has perimeter 8, side 4 has perimeter 16.
The ratio of perimeter to side stays fixed at 4:1 for every square, big or small.
For equilateral triangles the ratio of perimeter to side is always 3:1.
For a circle the same question becomes: is the ratio of circumference C to diameter D the same for all sizes?
slides.note: This ratio habit leads straight to pi.

slides.title: One Ratio for Every Circle
slides.kicker: Big or small, C over D never changes
bullets: In ancient days people realised that the ratio of circumference to diameter does not change if we change the size of the circle.
The book calls this the C/D ratio of the circle.
The whole game is to find its value: how would you estimate it?

slides.title: The Cotton Reel Experiment
slides.kicker: Thread, a reel, and pi at home
bullets: Measure the diameter D of a cotton reel as accurately as you can.
Tightly wrap very thin thread around the reel 20 times, unwrap, and measure the total length L.
Compute L/(20D): this is the C/D ratio you want.
Do you get a ratio between 3 and 4? Between 3.1 and 3.2? Please do the experiment!
slides.note: Ghar pe hi pi mil jayega!

slides.title: Meet Pi
slides.kicker: Say pie, not pizza
bullets: The C/D ratio is the famous constant we now call π, said as 'pie' and not as in 'pizza'.
π is a bridge between many different areas of mathematics.
It connects the straight-edged world of polygons with the infinite curves of nature.
Early civilisations relied on practical, good-enough values of π for construction and trade.

slides.title: Mesopotamia to Archimedes
slides.kicker: Pi's adventurous journey through history
bullets: In Mesopotamia, c. 1900 BCE, mathematicians moved beyond the crude integer value 3.
A circle's perimeter is slightly larger than its inscribed hexagon, so π > 3; they set π = 3 + 1/8 = 3.125.
By 250 BCE, Archimedes of Syracuse trapped π between the perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed polygons.
Hexagons gave 3 < π < 2 sqrt(3) ≈ 3.46, and Archimedes worked his way up to 96-sided polygons.

left.title: Mesopotamia, c. 1900 BCE
items: circle is bigger than inscribed hexagon

slides.note: The journey's destination: the exact formula of Mādhava.

slides.title: Half a Circle's Arc
slides.kicker: Fold the circle and count
bullets: A circle of diameter d has circumference πd; since the diameter is twice the radius, this is 2πr.
Reflect the circle in the diameter AB: the red and blue semicircles exchange places, so they have equal length.
Each semicircular arc is therefore 2πr ÷ 2 = πr.
Rotating the figure by 180° about the centre O gives the very same result.

slides.title: Quarter Circles Too
slides.kicker: A 90 degree turn shares the arc
bullets: Four quarter circles make a full circle.
Rotate the whole figure through 90°: each quarter circle moves and covers another quarter circle.
So each quarter-circle arc has the same length, 2πr ÷ 4 = πr/2.
These formulas also read 2πr × 180°/360° for the semicircle and 2πr × 90°/360° for the quarter circle.

slides.title: Any Arc, Any Angle
slides.kicker: The theta formula for curved pieces
bullets: An arc AB subtends an angle θ° at the centre O of the circle.
The arc is the fraction θ°/360° of the full circumference.
So the length of the arc is 2πr × θ°/360°.
Check it: θ = 180 gives πr, a semicircle; θ = 90 gives πr/2, a quarter circle.

items: arc AB subtends angle θ at centre O

slides.note: Fraction of the turn decides fraction of the arc.

slides.title: The 400 m Track
slides.kicker: Semicircles hiding in a race track
bullets: The track has two straight sections of 84.39 m each, and two curved portions that are semicircles with a common centre.
The innermost semicircle on each side has radius 36.5 m, and the width of each lane is 1.22 m.
An athlete running 0.3 m from the inner border covers two straights totalling 168.78 m.
Her two semicircular ends join into one circle of radius 36.5 + 0.3 = 36.8 m, about 231 m; the whole circuit is about 400 m.

items: curved ends: one circle of radius 36.8 m

slides.note: That is why it is called a 400 m track!

slides.title: Two Circles, One Puzzle
slides.kicker: Each circle passes through the other's centre
bullets: Two equal circles of radius r are placed so that each passes through the centre of the other, at A and B.
They intersect at C and D, and triangle ABC has AB = AC = BC = r, so it is equilateral.
Hence angle CAB = 60° and angle BAD = 60°, giving angle CAD = 120°.
Each dotted arc, the part lying inside the other circle, is 1/3 of the circumference of its circle.

items: angles at a centre add to 120°

slides.title: Counting the Red Arcs
slides.kicker: What remains after the dotted thirds
bullets: If each dotted arc is 1/3 of the circumference, each red arc is 2/3 of it.
One full circumference is 2πr, so each red arc measures (2/3) × 2πr.
The two red arcs together measure 2 × (2/3) × 2πr = 8πr/3.
slides.note: Draw it, then trust the angles.

slides.title: The Semicircle Paradox
slides.kicker: One big arc or three small ones?
bullets: Path 1 is one big semicircle a over PQ; path 2 is three semicircles b, c and d over the same PQ.
With radii a', b', c' and d', the lengths are πa' and π(b' + c' + d').
PQ equals both 2a' and 2b' + 2c' + 2d', so a' = b' + c' + d'.
The two paths have exactly equal length. Surprise!
slides.note: Same endpoints, same length: count on algebra.

slides.title: From Boundary to Space
slides.kicker: Area counts the space inside
bullets: From perimeter we move to area, the amount of space occupied by a two-dimensional region in a plane.
Measurement is always relative to something we call a unit.
For area the unit is a 1 × 1 square, whose area is taken as 1 unit^2, also written 1 sq. unit.

slides.title: Tiling with Unit Squares
slides.kicker: Rows times columns of little squares
bullets: Cover a rectangle with unit squares: a squares in each row, b rows in all.
The count is a × b, so a rectangle with sides a units and b units has area ab sq. units.
You know this from Grade 8; tiling shows you why it works.

slides.title: Squares and Strips
slides.kicker: Special rectangles, same idea
bullets: A square of side a units is a rectangle with a = b, so its area is a^2 sq. units.
A strip 1 unit wide and b units long has area b sq. units.
One formula, ab, covers every rectangle.

slides.title: A Triangle in a Box
slides.kicker: Enclose it, then take half
bullets: To find a triangle's area, enclose the triangle in a rectangle with the same base b and height h.
Use the rectangle formula, then notice that the triangle fills exactly half of the rectangle.
So a triangle with base b units and height h units has area (1/2)bh sq. units.
For an obtuse triangle the base splits as b = b1 + b2, and the same halving works.

slides.title: Two Copies, One Parallelogram
slides.kicker: A slicker route to bh/2
bullets: Take two congruent copies of a triangle and fit them together.
They form a parallelogram with base b and height h, whose area is bh.
Matching angles, like angle B'C'A' with angle BCA, show why the sides fit parallel.
So each triangle is half the parallelogram: area = (1/2)bh.

items: get a parallelogram of area bh

slides.title: The Median Theorem
slides.kicker: One cut, two equal areas
bullets: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; AD is a median of triangle ABC.
With BC = 2a, the bases BD and DC are equal, and both small triangles have the same height h.
Each has area ah/2 sq. units, so the median splits the triangle into two equal areas.
Surprise: the two pieces are, in general, differently shaped!
slides.note: A theorem worth telling your friends.

slides.title: What Squaring Meant
slides.kicker: Build a square of equal area
bullets: In ancient times, to square a given shape meant to construct a square equal in area to that shape.
The shape could be a rectangle, a triangle, or a circle.
Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra (800 BCE) shows how to square a rectangle with sides a and b, where a > b.
The target: construct a square with area ab sq. units.

slides.title: Baudhāyana's Construction
slides.kicker: Ancient steps, still exact today
bullets: In rectangle ABCD with AD = a and AB = b, mark E on AD with AE = AB, and let F be the midpoint of ED.
Draw square AFGH with side AF and vertex H on AB produced.
Draw arc AG with centre H, cutting side BC at K.
Through K draw a line parallel to AH meeting GH at P; the square HPQS on HP has the same area as rectangle ABCD.

items: F is the midpoint of ED
arc from H cuts BC at K

slides.title: Why the Construction Works
slides.kicker: Pythagoras finishes the proof
bullets: From AE = b we get AF = (a + b)/2, and HK = (a + b)/2 as well, because HK is a radius of the arc.
Also BH = AH − AB = (a + b)/2 − b = (a − b)/2.
In the right-angled triangle HKP, the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem gives HP^2 = HK^2 − BH^2.
So HP^2 = ((a+b)/2)^2 − ((a-b)/2)^2 = ab, and square HPQS equals the rectangle in area.

slides.title: An Identity in Disguise
slides.kicker: Algebra you can draw with a compass
bullets: The construction is a geometrical translation of ((a+b)/2)^2 − ((a-b)/2)^2 = ab.
Notice how a difference of squares sits inside a compass-and-line drawing.
Think and Reflect: what procedure would you use to square a given triangle?

right.title: Geometry
items: HK minus BH in triangle HKP

slides.note: Baudhāyana draws the difference of two squares!

slides.title: Humans Love Circles
slides.kicker: Rope, peg, and thousands of years
bullets: A circle is extremely basic: with a rope and a peg to tie it to, you can draw one.
Human beings have used the circular shape in settlements, buildings and tools for thousands of years.
They needed circle areas for cylindrical grain towers, circular gardens and buildings, for planning cities and for tax purposes.

slides.title: Scaling Keeps Ratios
slides.kicker: Why C squared over A must be fixed
bullets: For a square of side a: perimeter P = 4a and area A = a^2, so P^2 : A = 16a^2 : a^2 = 16 : 1.
This ratio is 16 : 1 for all squares; it does not depend on the size of the square.
For an equilateral triangle, P^2 : A is likewise one fixed value for all sizes.
As we change the scale of any shape, the ratio P^2 : A depends only on the shape, not on its scale.

slides.title: Babylonians and Egyptians
slides.kicker: Two ancient formulas for circle area
bullets: For a circle too, the ratio C^2 : A must be some fixed constant.
Well before 1500 BCE, Babylonians measured the constant as close to 12, giving the formula A ≈ C^2/12.
Around 1500 BCE, Egyptians came up with A ≈ (8d/9)^2, where d is the diameter of the circle.
Since d = 2r, the Egyptian formula works out to about 3.16 r^2, much more accurate.

slides.title: Landing on πr^2
slides.kicker: The ratio story meets pi
bullets: The circumference is C = 2πr, so C^2 = 4π^2 r^2.
The fixed ratio works out to C^2 : A = 4π : 1, about 12.57 : 1, close to the Babylonian 12 : 1.
Solving gives the area of a circle: A = C^2/(4π) = πr^2 sq. units.
From the insect's walk to Mādhava's exact formula, the circle is now fully measured.
slides.note: Spot the gap, ask the question: that is how the book teaches.

flashcards.front: What is the perimeter of a shape?
flashcards.back: The total length around its border, like an insect's full walk around the shape back to its starting point.

flashcards.front: What is the perimeter of a rectangle with length a and width b?
flashcards.back: 2(a + b) units. The square formula 4a is the special case a = b.

flashcards.front: What ratio of perimeter to side does every square have?
flashcards.back: 4:1. It stays fixed whether the square grows larger or smaller.

flashcards.front: What do we call the perimeter of a circle?
flashcards.back: The circumference. The book then asks: is the ratio of circumference C to diameter D the same for circles of all sizes?

flashcards.front: What is the C/D ratio of a circle?
flashcards.back: The ratio of its circumference to its diameter. It does not change when the size of the circle changes.

flashcards.front: In the cotton reel experiment, what do you compute?
flashcards.back: L/(20D), where L is the length of thread wrapped tightly 20 times around a reel of diameter D.

flashcards.front: What value of π did Mesopotamian mathematicians use around 1900 BCE?
flashcards.back: 3 + 1/8 = 3.125, since the circle is slightly larger than its inscribed hexagon, so π must be larger than 3.

flashcards.front: How did Archimedes trap the value of π?
flashcards.back: Between the perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed polygons; hexagons gave 3 < π < 2 sqrt(3) ≈ 3.46.

flashcards.front: What is the circumference of a circle of radius r?
flashcards.back: 2πr units. In terms of the diameter d it is πd, and d = 2r.

flashcards.front: What is the arc length of a semicircle of radius r?
flashcards.back: πr, because reflecting in the diameter swaps the two equal semicircular arcs: 2πr ÷ 2 = πr.

flashcards.front: What is the length of an arc subtending θ° at the centre?
flashcards.back: 2πr × θ°/360°, the same fraction of the circumference as the angle is of a full turn.

flashcards.front: Why does a track runner's curved distance form one full circle?
flashcards.back: The two curved ends are semicircles with a common centre, so together they make one circle of radius 36.8 m (36.5 + 0.3).

flashcards.front: In the two-circle puzzle, why is angle CAD 120°?
flashcards.back: Triangle ABC has all sides r, so it is equilateral; angle CAB = 60° and angle BAD = 60° add up to 120°.

flashcards.front: What is the total length of the two red arcs in the two-circle puzzle?
flashcards.back: 8πr/3, because each red arc is 2/3 of a circumference 2πr, and there are two of them.

flashcards.front: One semicircle or three: which path from P to Q is longer?
flashcards.back: Neither. The radii satisfy a' = b' + c' + d', so πa' = π(b' + c' + d'): the two paths are equal.

flashcards.front: What does area measure?
flashcards.back: The amount of space occupied by a two-dimensional region in a plane.

flashcards.front: What is the unit of area?
flashcards.back: A 1 × 1 square; its area is taken as 1 unit^2, also written 1 sq. unit.

flashcards.front: What is the area of a rectangle with sides a and b?
flashcards.back: ab sq. units, found by tiling with unit squares: a squares per row and b rows.

flashcards.front: What is the area of a square of side a?
flashcards.back: a^2 sq. units. A square is just a rectangle whose length and width are both a.

flashcards.front: What is the area of a triangle with base b and height h?
flashcards.back: (1/2)bh sq. units, half the area of the rectangle or parallelogram that encloses it.

flashcards.front: How do two congruent copies of a triangle give its area?
flashcards.back: They fit together to make a parallelogram of area bh, so one triangle is half of it.

flashcards.front: What does a median of a triangle do to its area?
flashcards.back: It divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area, even though the two pieces are usually differently shaped.

flashcards.front: What did 'to square a shape' mean in ancient times?
flashcards.back: To construct a square equal in area to that shape, whether the shape was a rectangle, a triangle or a circle.

flashcards.front: Whose 800 BCE text shows how to square a rectangle?
flashcards.back: Baudhāyana's, in his Śhulbasūtra. It builds a square with the same area ab as a rectangle with sides a and b.

flashcards.front: Which identity is Baudhāyana's construction a picture of?
flashcards.back: ((a+b)/2)^2 − ((a-b)/2)^2 = ab, read off the right triangle HKP using the Baudhāyana-Pythagoras theorem.

flashcards.front: In the construction, what are HK and BH in terms of a and b?
flashcards.back: HK = (a+b)/2, being a radius, and BH = (a-b)/2, so HP^2 = HK^2 − BH^2 = ab.

flashcards.front: For any square, what is the ratio P^2 : A?
flashcards.back: 16 : 1, whatever its size, since P = 4a and A = a^2.

flashcards.front: What was the Babylonian formula for the area of a circle?
flashcards.back: A ≈ C^2/12, from measuring that the ratio C^2 : A is close to 12 : 1, well before 1500 BCE.

flashcards.front: What was the Egyptian area formula for a circle, around 1500 BCE?
flashcards.back: A ≈ (8d/9)^2, where d is the diameter; it is much more accurate than the Babylonian formula.

flashcards.front: What is the area of a circle of radius r?
flashcards.back: A = πr^2 sq. units. With C = 2πr, the fixed ratio C^2 : A works out to 4π : 1.

quiz.why: Perimeter of a square is 4 × side, and 4 × 5 = 20 cm.

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle has side 7 cm. What is its perimeter?
quiz.why: The ratio of perimeter to side is 3:1, so 3 × 7 = 21 cm.

the diameter grows more slowly than the area

examples.title: One Lap of the 400 m Track
examples.problem: A 400 m athletics track has two straight sections of 84.39 m each. The two curved ends are semicircles with a common centre, and the innermost semicircle on each side has radius 36.5 m. An athlete runs one complete circuit keeping 0.3 m from the inner border. What total distance does she run? (Use π = 22/7.)
steps: Straight sections: she runs 2 × 84.39 = 168.78 m in all.
Her curved path lies 0.3 m outside the inner border, so it is a circle of radius 36.5 + 0.3 = 36.8 m.
The two semicircular ends join into one full circle: 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 36.8 = 1619.2/7 ≈ 231.31 m.
examples.answer: About 400 m, which is exactly why the track is called a 400 m track.

examples.title: Arcs of Two Overlapping Circles
examples.problem: Two circles of equal radius 7 cm are placed so that each passes through the centre of the other. Find the total length of the two big arcs of the shape they form, ignoring the dotted portions inside, using π = 22/7.
steps: Let the centres be A and B and an intersection point C. Then AB = AC = BC = 7 cm, so triangle ABC is equilateral and angle CAB = 60°.
The same holds on the other side, so angle CAD = 60° + 60° = 120°, which is 1/3 of a full turn.
So each dotted arc is 1/3 of a circumference, and each red arc is 2/3 of a circumference.
One circumference: 2πr = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 cm, so each red arc is (2/3) × 44 = 88/3 cm.
Total of the two red arcs: 2 × 88/3 = 176/3 ≈ 58.7 cm. In symbols, 2 × (2/3) × 2πr = 8πr/3.
examples.answer: 8πr/3, which for r = 7 cm is 176/3, about 58.7 cm.

examples.title: A Median Cuts Area in Half
examples.problem: In triangle ABC, AD is the median to side BC. BC = 14 cm and the height from A to BC is 6 cm. Find the area of each of triangles ABD and ACD, and check that they are equal.
steps: AD is a median, so D is the midpoint of BC: BD = DC = 14 ÷ 2 = 7 cm.
Both small triangles have the same height h = 6 cm on equal bases of 7 cm.
Area of ABD = (1/2) × 7 × 6 = 21 sq. cm; area of ACD = (1/2) × 7 × 6 = 21 sq. cm.
Check: together they give 42 sq. cm, which equals (1/2) × 14 × 6, the area of the whole triangle.
examples.answer: Each part has area 21 sq. cm; the median divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area.

examples.title: Area of a Circular Garden
examples.problem: A circular garden has a diameter of 14 m. Using π = 22/7, find its circumference and its area.
steps: Ratio check: C^2 : A = 44^2 : 154 = 1936 : 154 ≈ 12.57 : 1, matching the exact constant 4π : 1 ≈ 12.57 : 1 (the Babylonians measured it as about 12 : 1).
examples.answer: Circumference 44 m and area 154 sq. m.
